title: What Does China Want?
gist: In this Foreign Affairs podcast interview ahead of the September 2026 Trump-Xi summit, Jessica Chen Weiss argues China's 2025 weaponization of rare-earth export controls succeeded not because of a decades-long master plan but because of accumulated, reactive learning from U.S. sanctions since the first Huawei action, that Washington badly underestimated its own interdependence with China (the 'pair of twos' misjudgment), and that lasting success requires abandoning zero-sum 'beat China' framing for a stable modus vivendi built on selective openness, credible mutual assurances on Taiwan, and continued U.S.-China cooperation on AI safety.

themes.theme: Collapse of the bipartisan hard-line China consensus

insights.claim: Weiss argues the bipartisan hard-line consensus on China that dominated U.S. policy discourse through the end of Trump's first term and the Biden administration was always shallower and more wobbly than it appeared, with broad concern about China but far less agreement on the exact shape of the challenge or the appropriate U.S. response.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Explains why Trump's dramatic policy reversal toward deal-making with China in his second term was possible -- the underlying bipartisan consensus was never as load-bearing as Washington insiders assumed, a useful lens for assessing how durable any future China-policy 'consensus' actually is.
insights.quote: I think that the consensus has come apart in ways that I didn't anticipate, although I think I wrote for Foreign Affairs on the eve of that election that the consensus was shallower and more wobbly than it appeared.
insights.locator: early exchange on the hard-line consensus

insights.claim: Weiss says Trump's second-term China policy has demonstrated that the prior hard-line consensus was far less constraining on a president than the Biden administration seemed to believe.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A framework for judging future U.S. presidents' latitude on China policy -- institutional/bipartisan 'consensus' narratives may constrain rhetoric more than actual presidential decision-making.
insights.quote: He has, I think, very much demonstrated that that consensus was not as constraining as his predecessor and the Biden administration seems to believe.
insights.locator: early exchange on the hard-line consensus

insights.claim: Weiss argues the Biden-era 'small yard, high fence' export-control strategy succeeded narrowly by its own stated metric (staying ahead at the AI model layer) but failed on the broader goal of slowing China's overall technological development, since China has flourished in AI adoption and open-source models and effectively indigenized around the constraints.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the effectiveness narrative around U.S. semiconductor/tech export controls -- suggests investors should not assume export-control regimes durably suppress Chinese tech-sector competitiveness, particularly in AI adoption and open-source ecosystems.
insights.quote: Efforts to slow China down may have constricted China's access to compute, for example, but they've been very effective indigenizing and finding other ways to accelerate China's modernization and development of essentially just as effective a tech stack.
insights.locator: exchange on the China Trap essay's legacy

insights.claim: Weiss says U.S. public opinion has shifted toward wanting to resolve conflicts with China through cooperation rather than containment, partly because more Americans recognized the U.S. and China came dangerously close to actual war in the Asia-Pacific or an economic meltdown during the prior year's trade and export-control war.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A shift in domestic U.S. sentiment toward cooperation over containment could sustain political space for continued U.S.-China de-escalation beyond the current administration.
insights.quote: Public opinion has shifted in the direction of wanting to resolve conflicts with China through one survey called cooperation and not through containing China's influence.
insights.locator: exchange on why the consensus shifted

themes.theme: How China's rare-earth weapon actually emerged

insights.claim: Weiss's core historical finding (from her Foreign Affairs piece with Gloria Xiong) is that China's dominance over rare-earth and permanent-magnet supply chains was not the result of a grand, farsighted strategic scheme to hold the world hostage, but emerged from market economics -- rare earths are polluting and costly to process, so developed countries shifted production to China by the 1990s.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Corrects a widely held 'deliberate 30-year plan' narrative about Chinese rare-earth dominance -- important for accurately modeling how quickly (or slowly) alternative, non-China rare-earth supply chains could actually be built, since the dominance was market-driven rather than engineered from the start.
insights.quote: Even though China has sought to take advantage of its position, its dominance is not the result of a grand farsighted scheme to hold the world hostage.

insights.claim: China dominates roughly 80 to 85 percent of global production of permanent magnets made with rare-earth minerals, with dependence particularly acute for certain rare earths like yttrium where there is no clear timeline for reducing single-source reliance on China.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A precise, current market-share figure (80-85%) that quantifies the scale of Western/allied vulnerability in rare-earth supply chains -- a foundational data point for any critical-minerals investment thesis.
insights.quote: China dominates the vast majorities, like 80 to 85 percent, especially of permanent magnets made with these rare earth minerals.
insights.locator: exchange on China's rare earth dominance

insights.claim: As late as 2010, Chinese rare-earth production exceeded official quotas by more than 35 percent due to widespread illegal mining operations, leading some observers to conclude that China's real competition in rare earths was crime rings inside its own borders rather than foreign buyers.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Reveals that China's own rare-earth industry was chaotic and poorly controlled as recently as 2010, undermining any narrative of a coordinated, top-down strategic buildup -- relevant context for assessing how consolidated (or fragile) China's current export-control enforcement apparatus actually is.
insights.quote: Even as late as 2010, production of rare earths exceeded quotas by more than 35 percent, suggesting that the government really struggled to reign in many of these illegal operations.
insights.locator: exchange on historical rare earths regulation

insights.claim: The 2010 China-Japan rare-earth export restriction, widely remembered as Beijing's first deliberate use of the 'rare-earth weapon,' actually originated with subnational port administrators trying to show displeasure over Japan's arrest of a fishing boat captain -- not a central strategic decision -- according to research by geographer Julie Klinger that Weiss cites.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Reframes a foundational case study in geoeconomic-coercion literature: the first apparent use of the rare-earth weapon was likely bureaucratic improvisation, not centralized Beijing strategy -- a caution against overreading intentionality into China's economic-coercion track record.
insights.quote: It wasn't clearly the result of a strategic decision by Beijing, that in fact, research by the geographer Julie Klinger suggested that actually it was in the context of this geopolitical tiff between Japan and China, that there were actually subnational officials, port administrators that thought that this would be a good way to show China's displeasure.

insights.claim: China's full 2025 escalation to extraterritorial rare-earth export controls (blocking third countries from re-exporting products containing Chinese-sourced materials to the U.S.) was triggered specifically by the Trump administration's expansion of chip and manufacturing-equipment export controls, not by tariffs alone.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise trigger mechanism (export-control expansion, not tariffs) for China's most severe economic-coercion tool to date -- critical for policymakers calibrating future sanctions to avoid re-triggering extraterritorial retaliation.
insights.quote: It wasn't even the tariffs, it was actually the export controls and their expansion that led China to unveil its own extraterritorial set of export controls.

insights.claim: It took three successive U.S. administrations' worth of sanctions and export-control actions -- starting with the first Trump administration's actions against Huawei -- for China to fully plan, prepare for, and eventually deploy its rare-earth 'break glass' playbook.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Establishes a multi-administration causal chain of escalation, useful for tracing how today's economic-coercion tools trace back to specific origin points (the Huawei action) -- relevant for anticipating what future U.S. actions might similarly provoke delayed retaliation.
insights.quote: It was really over three successive U.S. administrations that China first really decided to embrace this, explored it, prepared for it, and then finally unleashed it.
insights.locator: exchange on the timeline of Chinese rare earths strategy

insights.claim: Weiss cites Henry Farrell's observation that policymakers often do not realize how significant a supply-chain pain point is until the target is actually forced to activate it -- U.S. industries may have understood rare-earth/magnet supply-chain fragility, but policymakers broadly did not grasp how acute the pain would be until China's export stoppage actually happened.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A generalizable framework (opaque supply chains hide true vulnerability until coercion is applied) applicable well beyond rare earths -- relevant to stress-testing any critical-input dependency before an adversary tests it.
insights.quote: Often you don't realize where the pain points are and just how significant they are until you force the target to activate them.

insights.claim: Weiss says Treasury Secretary Bessent's 'pair of twos' framing at the outset of the 2025 trade war -- the belief that China would be forced to fold because it held a weak hand -- badly misjudged the reality of deep mutual U.S.-China interdependence.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A specific, named policy misjudgment (Bessent's 'pair of twos' remark) that investors and policymakers should treat as a case study in the risk of underestimating an adversary's leverage in an economically interdependent relationship.
insights.quote: The belief in escalation dominance, that we have it and they're just going to fold like Secretary Bessent said at the outset of the trade war, that China holds a pair of twos and so we can force them to back off. That just doesn't really capture reality.

insights.claim: Weiss recommends the U.S. pursue what Dalip Singh calls a 'shared doctrine of restraint' with China rather than either seeking full economic insulation/decoupling or searching for a new unilateral coercive 'ace card' to play against Beijing.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A named alternative policy framework ('shared doctrine of restraint') that could anchor future bilateral negotiations on export controls and sanctions -- a concept investors should watch for uptake in actual U.S. policy statements.
insights.quote: What we should instead be focused more on is developing what Dalip Singh called a shared doctrine of restraint.

insights.claim: Weiss argues 'a little diversification goes a long way' in reducing rare-earth dependence -- full independence from China is unrealistic given China's processing know-how and academic pipeline advantage, but even partial diversification meaningfully reduces the risk of overdependence-driven Chinese hubris or repeated weaponization.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for critical-minerals investment theses: the policy/investment goal should be meaningful partial diversification, not full reshoring, which is a more achievable and quicker-payoff target for capital allocation.
insights.quote: A little diversification goes a long way, and so actually remaining dependent to some extent is not as much of a problem. It's a problem when it's overdependent.

insights.claim: Weiss notes China's own bureaucracy was understaffed to administer its new rare-earth export-licensing regime when it announced the 2025 restrictions, meaning China itself is still building out the administrative capacity to both allow and restrict exports under the new licensing system.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Suggests China's rare-earth export-control regime has real implementation friction and is not a smoothly functioning coercive lever -- a potential source of delay, inconsistency, or unintended supply disruption that companies dependent on Chinese rare-earth exports should monitor.
insights.quote: One of the things that we talk about is how understaffed China's bureaucracy was at the time that they announced these export restrictions as licensing regime.

insights.claim: Japan has reduced its reliance on Chinese rare-earth and permanent-magnet supply from about 90 percent to roughly 60 percent since the 2010 crisis first galvanized the country's diversification debate.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A concrete, trackable benchmark (90% to 60% dependence reduction over ~15 years) for how long and how far meaningful rare-earth diversification realistically takes even for a committed, well-resourced country -- a pace-setter for evaluating U.S./allied diversification claims.
insights.quote: Since 2010, Japan has gone from a 90 percent reliance to something like a 60 percent reliance on the Chinese supply of rare earths and permanent magnets.

insights.claim: Weiss's forthcoming book (Oxford, February 2027) argues China wants sovereignty, security, and development -- a conservative, state-centric international order where countries are free from foreign interference and subversion, sovereignty is paramount, and the state is the ultimate arbiter of internal affairs, privileging state authority over individual political rights.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A core analytical framework for interpreting Chinese foreign policy across issues (Xinjiang, Hong Kong, Taiwan, UN diplomacy) -- useful lens for forecasting Chinese positioning on any new international governance question.
insights.quote: What China wants... is sovereignty, security and development... It's one that is where states are pretty much free to run their own affairs internally as they like.
insights.locator: exchange on China's vision of world order

insights.claim: Weiss describes China's preferred order as 'China first' but 'permissive of America first' -- China does business with governments of any political stripe as long as they don't run afoul of China's parochial interests (Xinjiang, Hong Kong, Taiwan), making it a nationalist/particularist rather than universalist model of leadership, unlike the Soviet Union's or Maoist China's ideological universalism.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Predicts China will not aggressively export an ideological model the way the USSR did -- relevant for assessing the actual risk of a global 'autocracy bloc' narrative versus a more transactional, sovereignty-respecting Chinese diplomatic posture.
insights.quote: This is a more nationalist or particularist form of leadership rather than the kind of universalism that the United States or even the Soviet Union or Maoist China, I think once subscribed to.
insights.locator: exchange on China's vision of world order

insights.claim: Weiss observes a growing recognition within China that the world is looking to it to fill 'global governance deficits' (Xi Jinping's own term), evidenced by China signaling willingness to reconsider privileges it holds at the WTO and efforts to lead multilaterally, such as through the World AI Conference.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: An early signal that China may be shifting from a purely self-interested global posture toward assuming more multilateral leadership responsibilities -- worth monitoring for whether China begins offering substantive concessions in international institutions like the WTO.
insights.quote: They've already signaled, for example, that they'd be willing to reconsider some of the privileges granted them previously at the WTO.
insights.locator: exchange on China filling governance deficits

insights.claim: A Chinese government adviser described China's post-'graduation' mindset to Weiss using an analogy: having spent years focused on resisting perceived U.S. containment and encirclement like a student trying to graduate, China now feels it has fought the U.S. to a standstill and faces open-ended strategic choices about what role to play next.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A vivid, sourced anecdote suggesting China's internal strategic debate is genuinely unsettled post-2025 trade war -- implying more unpredictability (not more confidence/aggression) in China's near-term global posture than a triumphalist narrative would suggest.
insights.quote: China has been like a student trying to graduate and very, very focused... Now that China in this metaphor or analogy has graduated, there's a whole range of choices available and there are real trade-offs.

insights.claim: Weiss criticizes Trump's approach to Taiwan as making apparently unilateral concessions -- including the largest-ever arms sale being postponed and treated as a bargaining chip -- without a real strategic conversation about what concessions China should give in return, calling it a missed opportunity.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Flags a specific, checkable policy critique (unreciprocated arms-sale concessions) relevant to assessing whether the upcoming Trump-Xi summit produces genuinely balanced or one-sided outcomes on Taiwan.
insights.quote: This willingness to make what are apparently unilateral concessions without a real strategic conversation about the concessions that China needs to make in return, I think is a real missed opportunity.
insights.locator: exchange on what Trump is getting wrong

insights.claim: Weiss recommends that in exchange for continuing to pause further arms sales, the U.S. should ask China for a reciprocal pullback of military operations across the center line of the Taiwan Strait, an idea she previously argued for with Bonnie Glaser and Thomas Christensen.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A specific, concrete, and monitorable proposed concession (PLA pullback from the Strait median line) that would signal genuine two-sided de-escalation if adopted at the September 2026 summit.
insights.quote: Asking that China, in exchange for this continued pause, pull back its military operations across the center line of the Taiwan Strait... is that assurances from the Chinese side are necessary in order to prevent this action-reaction spiral from escalating.
insights.locator: exchange on concessions to seek from China

insights.claim: Weiss says China has not exploited what many saw as diminished U.S. credibility and resolve on Taiwan to attack the island, reflecting analyst John Culver's framing that Taiwan is 'a crisis to be avoided rather than an opportunity to be seized' for Beijing, especially amid China's own upheaval from purging its most senior military officers.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Directly counters the fear that reduced U.S. deterrence credibility on Taiwan (arms-sale delays, U.S. munitions depleted in Iran) will trigger near-term Chinese military action -- an important calming data point for Taiwan-conflict-risk premium in markets.
insights.quote: That reflects a deeper judgment that, as John Culver has said, Taiwan is a crisis to be avoided rather than an opportunity to be seized. And that... I don't think that the consequences are as immediate as many, I think, fear.

insights.claim: Weiss explicitly downplays the significance of reduced U.S. military readiness in the Pacific (no aircraft carrier in the region, depleted munitions from the Iran war) as a trigger for Chinese action on Taiwan, saying the underlying risk 'wasn't so great to begin with that now it has tipped the scales.'
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Pushes back against a military-balance-centric view of Taiwan invasion risk, arguing the decision is fundamentally political rather than driven by opportunistic military-balance calculations -- relevant for calibrating how much weight to put on U.S. force-posture changes as a Taiwan-conflict indicator.
insights.quote: I'm just saying that the risk may be higher, but it wasn't so great to begin with that now it has tipped the scales.

insights.claim: Weiss flags 2028 -- when the U.S., Taiwan, and possibly a reelected pro-independence-leaning DPP in Taiwan all hold elections -- as a moment analysts worry could unsettle the current relative calm around cross-strait tensions, more so than the previously feared 2027 window.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Shifts the market-relevant 'Taiwan flashpoint' calendar risk window from 2027 to 2028, tied to concrete election cycles in both Taipei and Washington -- a specific date to track for Taiwan Strait geopolitical risk premium.
insights.quote: There's a sense in the debate that, whereas we used to be very focused on 2027 as the moment of great risk, it's now 2028 when there'll be a presidential election in the United States, also one in Taiwan.
insights.locator: exchange on 2028 risk (Kurtz-Phelan's framing, affirmed by Weiss)

insights.claim: Weiss cites emerging research suggesting Xi Jinping genuinely believes in 'peaceful reunification' with Taiwan and is not the most hawkish voice in China favoring military force, though the debate within China is over tactics for reunification, not whether it should be the objective at all.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A meaningful nuance for war-risk modeling: the debate inside China's leadership is about method and timeline, not about whether unification is the goal -- implying Xi personally may not be the proximate driver of near-term military-option escalation.
insights.quote: There's important research suggesting that Xi Jinping actually believes in peaceful reunification... Xi Jinping is not the most hawkish voice urging the use of military force in China.
insights.locator: exchange on Xi Jinping and reunification

insights.claim: Weiss argues that framing U.S.-China relations around Taiwan as 'strategic competition' is itself dangerous, because it turns Taiwan into 'a prize to be won,' making Beijing believe there's no peaceful resolution path and pushing Washington toward pulling Taiwan further from China -- undermining the credibility of assurances needed to avoid conflict.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: A specific rhetorical/framing critique with direct policy implications: the language used by U.S. officials to describe the Taiwan issue can itself become a self-fulfilling escalatory mechanism, independent of actual military moves.
insights.quote: I find the language of strategic competition really problematic because the United States and China are not competing over Taiwan. And the more that we talk about this as a competition, then Taiwan is a prize to be won.

themes.theme: US-China AI safety cooperation as a bright spot

insights.claim: Weiss identifies U.S.-China cooperation on AI safety as one of the only areas where both the Biden and Trump administrations have shown genuine willingness in talks with Chinese officials to jointly manage a shared, urgent risk lacking settled rules of the road.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Identifies AI safety as a rare, bipartisan-durable channel for substantive U.S.-China engagement that has survived the transition between administrations -- a signal worth tracking for any formal AI-safety agreements emerging from the September 2026 Trump-Xi summit.
insights.quote: I think that's an important area for the two countries to continue to engage in substantive conversations about how they each see the respective risks and what steps they might be willing to take separately or together.

themes.theme: China's domestic constraints and the Russia relationship

insights.claim: Weiss argues China's failure to more aggressively capitalize on growing global skepticism of the U.S. stems partly from uncertainty about how long the current U.S.-China truce will last, making Chinese strategists reluctant to distance themselves from strategic partners like Russia that serve as a hedge/buffer against renewed U.S. pressure.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Explains why the deepening China-Russia relationship persists even when it damages China's European reputation -- China views Russia as insurance against a possible U.S. policy 'snapback,' a durable structural reason not to expect Sino-Russian distancing soon.
insights.quote: In a world of U.S. supremacy and willingness to put great pressure on both China and Russia, the two have looked to each other as sources of ballast and insurance.

insights.claim: Weiss ties China's continued closeness with Russia and its reluctance to rebalance toward domestic consumption (away from export-driven growth) to the same underlying cause: Xi Jinping's ideological preference against the painful internal changes needed to reduce both external dependencies and domestic economic imbalances.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Links China's export-driven growth model persistence and its geopolitical alignment choices to the same root ideological cause -- suggesting neither the 'second China shock' export glut nor the Russia relationship will resolve without a deeper internal Chinese policy shift.
insights.quote: This is bound up with their, particularly Xi Jinping's, unwillingness to do more to rebalance internally away from exports as a driver or sustainer of growth and more toward domestic consumption in households.
insights.locator: exchange on China's lack of recalibration

insights.claim: Weiss says China is not seeking to grab the 'brass ring' of global supremacy as the U.S. steps back from leadership -- China remains cautious about assuming global burdens or making concessions necessary to earn broader international trust, even as it gains favorability in global polling.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Directly counters a 'China is seizing the moment to replace U.S. global leadership' narrative -- suggests investors should not price in an assertive Chinese leadership vacuum-fill scenario in the near term.
insights.quote: The United States is taking itself out of the number one position, but China is not clearly grabbing that brass ring. China is moving much more, looking for opportunities, but I think largely cautious.
insights.locator: exchange on China missing a moment of opportunity

themes.theme: Defining success in the US-China relationship

insights.claim: Weiss defines a successful outcome for U.S. China policy not as 'beating China' but as reaching a new modus vivendi that secures American interests in affordability, stable and secure supply chains, cheap clean energy, and domestic innovation, while still enabling international cooperation on shared challenges.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Offers a concrete, non-zero-sum success metric for U.S. China policy that investors can use to judge whether future U.S. administrations are pursuing pragmatic coexistence versus unproductive maximalist confrontation.
insights.quote: For me, success would look like a new modus vivendi or equilibrium that serves American interests in affordability, in stable and secure supply chains, in cheap, clean energy and a vibrant hub of innovation.

insights.claim: Weiss argues restoring people-to-people ties -- including welcoming Chinese students, which Trump himself has said is good for American universities even as his administration acts less welcoming in practice -- is an important, low-cost area for stabilizing the U.S.-China relationship given growing societal estrangement between the two countries.
insights.speaker: Jessica Chen Weiss
insights.so_what: Flags a concrete, trackable policy inconsistency (rhetorical openness to Chinese students vs. actual visa/administrative unwelcomeness) as a leading indicator of whether the U.S. is serious about stabilizing the broader relationship beyond trade and security.
insights.quote: This growing estrangement between the two societies... makes it really difficult even to understand what's happening in the other country, let alone benefit from the human talent that really wants to leave China and go elsewhere.
